title: AYDAROV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
summary:
In Aydarov and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were two extended families of Bulgarian nationals of Roma ethnic origin—the Aydarovi and Ilievi families—living in the Kremikovtsi settlement near the village of Marchevo. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma families facing the demolition of their homes, which were built without official permits on municipal land, in a settlement inhabited exclusively by Roma and established in the late 1960s. The applicants, including children with serious health conditions, lived in basic brick houses that were subject to demolition orders issued by the Bulgarian authorities between 2010 and 2011, after inspections found the buildings to be unlawful. While one family sought judicial review of the demolition order, the other did not, and neither succeeded in preventing the orders from becoming final.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), arguing that the demolition orders and their enforcement were disproportionate and failed to consider their individual circumstances. However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had not exhausted all available domestic remedies, as required by Article 35 of the Convention.

This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller families often face when seeking protection against forced evictions, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and legal exclusion across Europe.
